steps.title: Import TypeScript utilities
steps.instruction: Import TypeScript's built-in utility types for working with types.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in utility types from 'typescript'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a utility type
import { Partial } from 'typescript';
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have the necessary imports to use TypeScript's built-in utility types.
successCriteria: TypeScript utility types are imported from 'typescript'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported TypeScript's utility types. These will help us work with and transform types throughout this lesson.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing from the correct module and using the proper import syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement isn't quite right. Remember to import TypeScript's utility types from the 'typescript' module.

steps.title: Define a basic schema interface
steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript interface named 'Schema' that defines the structure of a schema object with properties and their types. The interface should have a 'properties' field that is a Record mapping string keys to string values representing types.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and define a 'properties' field with the type Record<string, string>.
steps.seedCode:
// Import TypeScript utility types here

// Define your Schema interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: A Schema interface is created with a properties field typed as Record<string, string>.
successCriteria: The Schema interface is defined with a 'properties' field of type Record<string, string>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the Schema interface with the correct structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface has a 'properties' field with the type Record<string, string>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Schema interface is not correctly defined. It should have a 'properties' field with type Record<string, string>.

steps.title: Create a simple type mapper function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'mapSchemaToType' that takes a generic parameter 'S' (which extends the Schema interface) and returns a mapped type based on that schema.
steps.hint: Start with 'function mapSchemaToType<S extends Schema>()' or use an arrow function with the same signature. The function should return a type, not a value.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function signature is defined that will later be used to map schema definitions to TypeScript types.
successCriteria: The function 'mapSchemaToType' is defined with a generic parameter 'S extends Schema' and returns a mapped type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the function signature correctly. This generic function will serve as the foundation for our type mapper.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function has a generic parameter 'S' that extends the Schema interface and returns a type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature doesn't match the requirements. It should take a generic parameter 'S extends Schema' and return a mapped type.

steps.title: Implement the basic type mapper
steps.instruction: Inside your mapSchemaToType function, implement the function body to return a mapped type that converts each schema property to a TypeScript type.
steps.hint: Use a mapped type to iterate over the keys of the schema and transform each property type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should have a proper implementation that returns a mapped type based on the schema parameter.
successCriteria: The mapSchemaToType function returns a mapped type that transforms schema properties
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the type mapper function using mapped types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the function returns a mapped type that transforms each property.
steps.feedbackWrong: The implementation doesn't match the expected pattern. Review how mapped types work in TypeScript.

steps.title: Add support for nested schemas
steps.instruction: Extend the Schema interface to support nested object schemas by making its property values accept either primitive types or other Schema objects.
steps.hint: Use a union type in the Schema interface to allow properties to be either primitive types (string, number, boolean) or nested Schema objects.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Schema interface will now support nested structures, allowing property values to be either primitive types or other Schema objects.
successCriteria: Schema interface uses a union type that includes Schema itself as a possible property type, enabling recursive/nested schemas.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully extended the Schema interface to support nested structures. This is a key step in building a flexible type mapper.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the Schema interface needs to explicitly allow Schema objects as property values. Try using a union type that includes 'Schema' itself.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Schema interface still only accepts primitive types. To support nested schemas, you need to modify the interface so property values can also be Schema objects.

steps.title: Implement array type support
steps.instruction: Update the Schema interface to support array types by allowing values to be arrays of strings, numbers, or booleans.
steps.hint: Modify the type annotation in the Schema interface to include arrays using the TypeScript syntax for array types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Schema interface now supports array types for its property values.
successCriteria: The Schema interface includes array types (string[], number[], boolean[]) in its union type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully extended the Schema interface to support array types, which is essential for handling more complex data structures.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to include all three array types (string[], number[], boolean[]) in the union type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Schema interface should allow array types. Check the union type to include string[], number[], and boolean[].

steps.title: Create union type support
steps.instruction: Extend the Schema interface to allow union types by modifying the property type to accept multiple possible primitive types.
steps.hint: Update the interface so each property can be a union of string, number, or boolean types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Schema interface now supports union types for its properties.
successCriteria: Schema interface property type is a union of string, number, and boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully extended the Schema interface to support union types, allowing each property to accept multiple primitive types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the property type in the Schema interface is a union of string, number, and boolean types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Schema interface property type should be a union of string, number, and boolean types.

steps.title: Add optional property support
steps.instruction: Update the Schema interface to mark properties as optional using the '?' modifier, then modify the mapSchemaToType function to handle optional properties by returning Partial<T>.
steps.hint: Use the '?' after property names in the interface to make them optional. In the function, you can use TypeScript's Partial utility type to map the schema to a type where all properties are optional.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Schema interface should allow optional properties, and mapSchemaToType should return a Partial<T> type to reflect optional properties in the mapped type.
successCriteria: Schema interface uses '?' for optional properties, and mapSchemaToType returns Partial<T>.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added support for optional properties in both the schema definition and the type mapper.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both the Schema interface and the mapSchemaToType function are updated to handle optional properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've used the '?' modifier in the Schema interface and that mapSchemaToType returns Partial<T>.

steps.title: Create validation examples
steps.instruction: Create two example schemas and validate that mapSchemaToType produces correct TypeScript types by adding console.log statements.
steps.hint: Define two schema objects with different structures (e.g., userSchema and productSchema) and log the result of calling mapSchemaToType with each.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will see the console output showing the mapped types for your example schemas, confirming the mapper works with real-world examples.
successCriteria: Two example schemas are defined and mapSchemaToType is called with each, with results logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created validation examples to test your type mapper.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you define two schemas and call mapSchemaToType with each, logging the results.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to create two example schemas and validate mapSchemaToType by logging the results.

steps.title: Export the final type mapper
steps.instruction: Export the Schema interface and mapSchemaToType function so they can be imported in other TypeScript modules.
steps.hint: Use the 'export' keyword before the interface and function declarations.
steps.expectedOutcome: The Schema interface and mapSchemaToType function are exported, making them available for import in other modules.
successCriteria: Schema interface and mapSchemaToType function are both exported using the 'export' keyword.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully exported the type mapper utilities. Now they can be imported and reused in other TypeScript files.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both the Schema interface and mapSchemaToType function are exported.
steps.feedbackWrong: The exports aren't quite right. Remember to use the 'export' keyword before both the interface and function declarations.
